content:
Apple today officially launched the "Apple Upgrade" rental program, operating largely as expected. While the program makes products more affordable on a monthly basis, it also risks trapping users in an endless rental cycle.

The reason is that, unlike the iPhone Upgrade Program it partially replaces, users do not own the device outright at the end of the lease period...

As Apple product prices continue to reach new highs, the appeal of making devices more affordable through this program is clear. Judging by the monthly payments alone, the Apple Upgrade program undoubtedly delivers on this front.

For example, you could rent a MacBook Pro with 16GB of memory and 1TB of storage for as little as $38.99 per month. This makes Apple products accessible to more consumers, which is undoubtedly a good thing.

The hidden concern of the Apple Upgrade program

However, the hidden concern is exactly what I anticipated last week: users will approach this program in exactly the same way as car leasing. While you have the option to pay a lump sum at the end of the lease to obtain full ownership of the car, almost no one actually does this. The vast majority of car lessees simply return the old car and lease a new one, starting the cycle all over again.

The Apple Upgrade program is likely to see the same pattern. To obtain full ownership of the product, you must pay a lump sum equal to the difference between the total amount you have already paid in lease installments and the device's original retail price.

Let's use the MacBook Pro mentioned above as an example to see how this works out (totals rounded to the nearest whole number):

36-month plan

  • Monthly payment: $38.99
  • Total paid over the lease term: $1,403
  • Lump sum required to obtain ownership of the machine: $585

24-month plan

  • Monthly payment: $53.99
  • Total paid over the lease term: $1,295
  • Lump sum required to obtain ownership of the machine: $703

For consumers who cannot afford to purchase the machine outright, these are not small amounts. Unless they set aside the relevant difference throughout the lease term, they are likely to find it difficult to cover. As a result, the most likely outcome is that they will start a new cycle all over again.

A smarter approach, if you can afford it

If you can afford a higher monthly payment, a smarter approach would be to simulate the workings of the old iPhone Upgrade Program yourself.

On one hand, you pay the lease amount to Apple; on the other, you simultaneously deposit a sum into a savings account each month to cover the final lump sum. Using the 36-month MacBook Pro lease as an example, the numbers would be as follows:

  • Monthly lease payment: $38.99
  • Monthly savings deposit: $16.26
  • Total monthly outlay: $55.25
  • Total paid to Apple: $1,403
  • Total saved toward the lump sum: $585.36 (plus any interest earned)

Featured comment posted by igorsky

This article (along with these highly critical comments) measures everyone by the same yardstick. Some people simply enjoy getting a new phone every year, and this program just makes it easier and more hassle-free to do so. If you buy a new phone with cash and sell the old one each year, the total outlay is actually comparable to leasing. Please stop assuming everyone has the same spending habits.

You can then use your savings to pay the $585 lump sum, and the machine is entirely yours, with no encumbrances.

Of course, if you do want to upgrade to a new machine, you can always sell your current machine, which is already yours, and start a new lease. The amount received from a private resale is very likely enough to cover the lump sum on the new contract, so you can simply deposit this amount into your savings account, leaving only the lease payment as your monthly outlay.

How do you plan to fund your future Apple purchases? Share your thoughts in the comments.
